data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Follow how body systems exchange materials and signals. The relay is a model: systems work continuously and overlap.

1. Read **The Relay Race** and trace oxygen from lung air sacs to a muscle cell.
2. Use the **Glossary**, **Matching**, and **Memory** games to practice the terms.
3. Study **Who Does What** and sort the jobs in **Which System Handles This?**. Explain how other systems can help.
4. Use **The Handoff Map** and **Cornell Notes** to connect ideas.
5. Complete the quiz, then review any answers you want to revise.
6. Create a cue in **Remember the Relay Team**. Explain both its usefulness and its limits.
7. Complete **Investigation: What Changes When You Move?** with the supplied fictional data. No exercise or personal measurements are needed.

You may write, speak, draw with explanations, or use your communication device. Use observations to support a claim and identify what remains uncertain.

history.title: The Relay Race
history.data:
## The Relay Race

A body **system** is a group of parts that work together. Several systems keep a muscle cell working. We can compare their shared jobs to a relay. But the systems work at the same time, not in separate turns.

The **respiratory** system moves air into the lungs. Tiny air sacs called alveoli have thin walls. **Oxygen** passes through these walls into nearby blood. Carbon dioxide moves the other way and leaves when we breathe out. Moving air and moving gases across a wall are different jobs.

The **circulatory** system moves blood. The heart is an **organ** that pumps it. Blood goes from the lungs to the left side of the heart, then toward body cells. It returns to the right side and goes to the lungs again. A blood **vessel** is a tube. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry it toward the heart. These names tell direction, not oxygen level. All human blood is red; blue in a diagram is a color code.

The **digestive** system breaks food into smaller parts. A **nutrient** is a substance the body needs. Most nutrients enter the body through the small intestine. Glucose enters blood; many dietary fats first enter lymph, then reach blood. Some nutrients supply energy; others help build or run the body. Lungs supply oxygen, not food.

Inside cells, one process uses oxygen and glucose to make ATP, which transfers energy for cell work. This process is called aerobic cellular respiration. It also makes carbon dioxide and water. Cells have other ways to make some ATP without oxygen.

The **nervous** system helps **coordinate** these jobs. Nerves send signals for movement and other tasks. Some quick reflexes use circuits in the spinal cord before we become aware of them. Do not test a reflex with a hot object.

The **skeletal** system supports the body and protects organs. A typical adult has about 206 bones, with some variation. Tendons join skeletal muscles to bones. The **muscular** system moves the body as muscles pull. Other muscles move food through organs or pump blood.

During activity, breathing and heart rate often rise. Nerves, hormones and local signals help match supply to need. Pacemaker cells in the heart start its beat; nerves adjust the rate. These six systems are part of a larger body with other linked systems too.

data.def: A group of parts that work together to do a job.
The breathing system — lungs that take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
The heart-and-blood system that delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells.
The system that breaks food into nutrients the body can absorb.
The system that sends signals to control and coordinate the body.
The system of bones that gives structure and protects organs.
Muscles that contract to move the body, move materials through organs and pump blood.
A gas used in aerobic cellular respiration to help transfer energy from food; not all cellular energy pathways require it.
A substance the body needs to work, grow or repair itself. Some provide energy; others have different jobs.
A body part made of tissues that does a specific job, like the heart.
A tube that carries blood through the body.
To make different parts work together at the right time.

data.title: Remember the Relay Team
data.instructions: Each card locks in facts from The Relay Race. Study the example aid, make it yours, and explain how it leads back to the way the systems hand off to each other.
data.sourceExcerpt: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood, which travels through the heart to tissues. Many nutrients enter blood through the small intestine; many fats enter lymph first. Nervous, hormonal and local signals coordinate responses. Muscles pull on skeletal attachments.

cards.target: The six systems and each one's job
essentialFacts: Respiratory: brings oxygen in and carbon dioxide out through the lungs.
Circulatory: the heart and vessels deliver oxygen and nutrients and carry waste away.
Digestion breaks food down; many nutrients enter blood and many fats enter lymph first.
Nervous signals use electrical activity and chemical communication to help coordinate the body.
A typical adult has about 206 bones; skeletal muscles pull on bones through tendons.

cards.target: The oxygen relay: lungs to blood to cell
essentialFacts: Air enters the lungs and oxygen crosses from tiny sacs called alveoli into the blood.

history.title: Systems Working Together

questions.question: Which system takes oxygen out of the air and passes it to the blood?
options: The digestive system
The skeletal system
The respiratory system
The muscular system

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the oxygen and glucose pathways described in the lesson?
options: Oxygen enters through the digestive system; glucose enters through the lungs
Both oxygen and glucose enter the blood directly from inhaled air
Glucose comes from bones; oxygen is made by the heart
Oxygen crosses from lung air sacs into blood; glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into blood
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen crosses from lung air sacs into blood; glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into blood

questions.question: You touch something hot and jerk your hand away before you even think. Which system made that happen so fast?
options: The nervous system
The digestive system
The respiratory system
The skeletal system

questions.question: Why is the body called 'a system of systems'?
options: Because each system works completely alone on its own separate job
Because the systems constantly work together and hand materials to each other
Because there is really one giant system with no separate parts inside
Because the systems compete with each other for the body's limited energy
questions.correctAnswer: Because the systems constantly work together and hand materials to each other

questions.question: When you sprint, your breathing AND your heartbeat both speed up. Why do BOTH change together?
options: The two systems are actually the same system with two different names
Only the heart really changes; breathing only seems faster because you notice it
The skeletal system forces them both to speed up when the bones move faster
Your muscles need more oxygen, so respiratory and circulatory systems ramp up together
questions.correctAnswer: Your muscles need more oxygen, so respiratory and circulatory systems ramp up together

questions.question: Trace one oxygen molecule from the air to a muscle cell, naming every system it passes through.
questions.expectedAnswer: Oxygen enters the respiratory airways, reaches an alveolus, diffuses into capillary blood, travels through pulmonary veins and the left heart, then body arteries and capillaries. It diffuses into muscle cells and is used in aerobic respiration. Coordination is important but is not another place the molecule passes through.

questions.question: Explain how the digestive and circulatory systems help deliver glucose from food to a working muscle. What does the muscle cell do with it?
questions.expectedAnswer: Digestion breaks down carbohydrates, and glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into blood. Circulation carries it to muscles. In aerobic cellular respiration, muscle cells use glucose and oxygen to make ATP for cell work, including contraction. Many dietary fats take a different initial route through lymph before reaching blood.

history.meta: 5 MCQ + 2 short answer • interaction is the target idea

data.title: Body Systems — The Team That Keeps You Alive

cues.text: How can breathing and circulation adjust during activity?

data.question: Why are there so many tiny blood vessels?
data.answer: Tiny vessels bring blood close to cells. Their thin walls let gases, nutrients and wastes pass between blood and tissues.

data.question: How fast do nerve signals travel? ⚡
data.answer: Speeds vary. A quick reflex can use a circuit in the spinal cord before you become aware of it. Signals also reach the brain. Never test this with a hot object.

data.question: Why does my heart beat faster when I am scared?
data.answer: Nerves and hormones can raise heart rate when you sense a threat. This helps prepare the body to act. The response can start before you choose what to do.

data.question: Do all my systems ever rest? 😴
data.answer: Some jobs slow down during sleep, but they do not all stop. Your heart still pumps and your lungs still move air.

data.question: How many bones do I have? 🦴
data.answer: A typical adult has about 206 bones. The count can vary. Some bones join as children grow, so age and how we count the parts matter.

data.question: Which system is the most important?
data.answer: The systems depend on one another. People can have different organs and abilities, sometimes with medical support. Study how the parts connect rather than ranking them.

data.title: What Changes When You Move?
data.instructions: Investigate the supplied fictional observations. Compare breathing and pulse estimates, connect the pattern to lesson facts, and explain what the numbers cannot show. No exercise or personal measurements are needed.
data.fitReason: Comparing two measurements gives students evidence to discuss interacting systems while distinguishing an observed pattern from a causal explanation.

brief.context: Fictional classroom dataset, invented for calculation practice; these are not measurements of real people or health targets. Three cases each have counts from matched 15-second windows at rest, just after one minute of gentle activity, and two minutes after activity ended. Each pair below is breaths / pulse beats. Case A: rest 4 / 18; just after 6 / 24; two minutes after 4 / 19. Case B: rest 3 / 17; just after 5 / 22; two minutes after 4 / 18. Case C: rest 4 / 20; just after 5 / 23; two minutes after 4 / 20. Multiply each count by four to estimate a rate per minute. These examples illustrate possible patterns, not predictions for every person.
brief.drivingQuestion: What changes appear in the fictional breathing and pulse counts, and how far can those observations support an explanation about interacting systems?
brief.seedDirection: Label the data fictional. Convert each 15-second count to a per-minute estimate, then compare each case with its own resting values.
lockedLessonFacts: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide through the lungs.
The circulatory system delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries waste away.
Aerobic respiration transfers energy from glucose using oxygen; muscle cells use ATP to contract.
Working muscles use more energy. Breathing and blood flow often increase to support oxygen delivery and carbon-dioxide removal.
Nervous, hormonal and local signals coordinate responses; these rate counts do not identify which signal came first.
openQuestions: How much does each estimated rate change from rest to just after activity?
At the two-minute observation, which estimates match the resting value and which remain higher?
Why can three observation times not establish the exact time of recovery or the order of coordinating signals?
criteria: A table of estimated breaths per minute and pulse beats per minute for all three fictional cases at all three times
A comparison of each case with its own resting values, with units shown
An explanation using respiratory and circulatory systems and their coordination, clearly separated from what was counted
One limit of the data and one follow-up question; explain relevant lesson vocabulary accurately
constraints: Use the supplied fictional data; no exercise or personal measurements are required.
Keep breaths per minute and pulse beats per minute in separate labeled columns.
Do not use the invented values to judge anyone's health, fitness, or expected response.
Do not claim the counts measure oxygen use, prove a causal mechanism, or reveal the first coordinating signal.
Complete in one class period; respond in writing, speech, drawings with explanations, or a communication device.
brief.deliverable: A labeled results table for the three fictional cases, a short explanation linking a pattern to lesson facts, and a statement of what remains unknown.

parallelExample.context: Fictional example: an animal model has 5 breaths counted in a 20-second window and 7 in another 20-second window.
parallelExample.move: A student multiplies each count by three: estimated rates are 15 and 21 breaths per minute. The estimate increased by 6 breaths per minute. The student reports the change but does not claim that the counts alone explain its cause.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Match the conversion to the counting window, retain units, and separate a numerical pattern from a causal explanation. Our main dataset uses 15-second windows, so its multiplier is four.

supports.frameStarter: In fictional Case ____, the estimated ____ rate changed from ____ to ____ per minute. This is consistent with ____. The counts alone cannot show ____.
frameChoices: Compare each case with its own resting estimates
Compare the two-minute estimate with rest without claiming an exact recovery time
Draw two graphs with separate labels and units
Explain how a counting error of one beat or breath changes a per-minute estimate
coachPrompts: Which part of your claim comes from the numbers, and which comes from the lesson?
Does a faster pulse directly measure the volume of blood pumped or the oxygen used?
Which questions would need different measurements or a different investigation?

data.coachHint: Use count × 4 for each 15-second sample. Compare like units, separate evidence from explanation, and state the limits of three fictional observation times.
data.sourceExcerpt: Activity changes oxygen delivery and waste-removal demands. Breathing and circulation often adjust together through nervous, hormonal and local signals.
